red.focus: Recognize different sources of legal authority
red.summary: Different legal systems may identify binding law through statutes, court decisions, custom, religious texts, or constitutions. Learn to ask who recognizes a source and which institution can apply it.
checklist: I can identify a legal source without assuming it is universal
I can separate written law from the institutions applying it
I can compare precedent and legislation without stereotyping jurisdictions

sections.title: A Rule Needs a Source
sections.body_md: Imagine a person asking whether a landlord can raise the rent. In one jurisdiction, legislation may state the main limits; in another, courts' interpretations of lease and property law may be crucial. A legal source is the recognized basis for a rule, such as a statute, judicial decision, constitution, or custom. The first task is not to memorize the names of legal families. It is to locate the jurisdiction and determine which institutions actually recognize and enforce the relevant sources.

sections.title: Common and Civil Law
sections.body_md: In common-law systems, judicial precedents can provide binding rules within a court hierarchy. Civil-law systems commonly give enacted codes a central organizing role, but courts still interpret law and their decisions can be influential. Neither label describes every rule in every country. England has extensive legislation, while civil-law jurisdictions develop bodies of case law. The useful distinction is how legal sources are identified, ranked, and reasoned from in a particular legal order.

sections.title: Custom and Religious Authority
sections.body_md: Some systems recognize customary practices or religiously grounded norms alongside state legislation. Their legal effect can depend on constitutions, statutes, personal-law arrangements, community institutions, or local recognition. A custom accepted within a community is not automatically enforceable in every national court; religious interpretation is also institutionally diverse. A careful lawyer avoids treating any entire religion or society as a single unchanging legal code. Ask who applies the rule, to whom, and by what recognized authority.

yellow.focus: Analyze hierarchies of authority in comparative systems
yellow.summary: Move beyond labels and map which sources prevail when they conflict. Learn why constitutional supremacy, legislative authority, and precedent operate differently across legal systems.
checklist: I can rank competing sources within a specified jurisdiction
I can distinguish binding from persuasive decisions
I can recognize the institutional role of judicial review

sections.title: Hierarchy Before Interpretation
sections.body_md: Suppose a regulation conflicts with a statute that authorizes it. A lawyer must first determine whether the regulation is valid under the higher rule. Other conflicts may involve constitutional provisions, treaties, or binding precedents. Source hierarchy supplies the order of legal authority, though that order differs by country. It is not enough to quote the most detailed rule: the rule must be issued by an institution empowered to make it and must survive applicable limits.

sections.title: Precedent Is Not Uniform
sections.body_md: A decision from a higher court may bind lower courts on a legal proposition essential to its result. The weight of precedent depends on jurisdiction, court structure, publication and the issue decided. Courts can distinguish different facts, and some may overrule earlier decisions under stated conditions. Civil-law jurisdictions also use prior decisions, often through a different institutional logic. The sophisticated question is what legal effect the specific decision has, not whether it comes from a so-called precedent country.

sections.title: Constitutions, Legislatures and Courts
sections.body_md: Where a constitution prevails over ordinary legislation, courts or other institutions may review whether a statute respects it. Other constitutional arrangements emphasize legislative sovereignty or varied forms of constitutional dialogue. A treaty may have direct effect in one legal order and require implementing legislation in another. When studying a new country, write a source map: constitution, legislation, delegated rules, decisions, recognized customs, and the institutions capable of resolving conflicts.

orange.focus: Compare overlapping state and nonstate legal orders
orange.summary: Analyze the authority of customary, Indigenous, religious and international norms within plural systems. Distinguish legitimacy claimed by a community from recognition by a state tribunal.
checklist: I can explain recognition of nonstate norms without equating all traditions
I can analyze conflicts between state and community legal institutions
I can identify treaty incorporation and direct-effect questions

sections.title: Plurality Is an Institutional Fact
sections.body_md: A land dispute may involve a national statute, Indigenous governance, and customary understandings of stewardship. Each source can carry meaning for the people concerned, but its effect in a state court depends on domestic constitutional or legislative arrangements and applicable agreements. Calling the situation pluralism does not solve which rule prevails. The lawyer must trace each authority claim, identify the recognized forum, and acknowledge where formal state law fails to capture the community's legal relationships.

The lawyer must trace each authority claim, identify the recognized forum, and acknowledge where formal state law fails to capture the community's legal relationships.

sections.title: International Law Enters Differently
sections.body_md: Two countries may ratify the same treaty but give it different domestic effects. In some systems a treaty provision can be directly invoked if legal conditions are met; in others legislation is required before domestic courts enforce it. Treaty interpretation also involves international rules that cannot be reduced to national precedent doctrine. Comparative analysis therefore separates the state's external obligation from the domestic procedural route available to an individual. Confusing the two can promise clients a remedy their courts cannot provide.

sections.title: Recognition Can Both Protect and Limit
sections.body_md: State recognition of customary law may preserve community authority, yet it can also freeze a living tradition into a narrow official definition. Religious or personal-law rules may similarly be applied through institutions with different procedures and accountability. An advanced lawyer asks who has standing to speak for the tradition, whether affected members can challenge interpretations, and how constitutional rights interact. Legal pluralism is not simply tolerance of difference; it is the design of fair relationships among institutions.

black.focus: Critique authority through pluralism and postcolonial legitimacy
black.summary: At doctoral depth, treat the identity of law's authoritative voice as a contested institutional and moral problem. Design comparative inquiry that respects legal difference without romanticizing any institution.
checklist: I can separate formal recognition from justified authority
I can evaluate state monopoly claims against Indigenous self-government
I can defend cross-system conflict rules with reasons and accountability

sections.title: Who Gets to Define Law?
sections.body_md: A national constitution may identify state institutions as the sole sources of enforceable law, while an Indigenous community understands its obligations through older legal practices. The positivist question asks what the state recognizes; the moral and comparative question asks whether exclusive state recognition is justified. Historical conquest can make that distinction especially important. A doctoral analysis must not simply treat state power as proof of legitimacy, nor imagine every community rule is beyond critique. Authority requires transparent justification to those governed.

sections.title: Comparison Is Not Ranking
sections.body_md: Legal-family labels can quietly place one tradition at the center and describe others only by how they differ. A better method compares problems, sources, institutions, access, remedies, and internal disagreement. The analyst should identify whose perspectives are missing from reported judgments and legal scholarship. For example, how a community resolves a family dispute cannot be understood solely from a national appellate judgment that later reviewed it. Comparative rigor requires multiple kinds of evidence and humility about translation.

sections.title: Designing a Fair Conflict Rule
sections.body_md: Imagine two legitimate institutions issuing incompatible decisions over the same ancestral land. An adequate framework must identify jurisdictional claims, participation of affected people, governing rights, and a lawful method of coordinating remedies. Centralized supremacy can create predictability but silence local authority; unchecked fragmentation may leave vulnerable people without reliable redress. A defensible proposal specifies why one forum decides, when consultation or consent is required, and who may review the outcome. Comparative law becomes worthwhile when it protects lives rather than merely cataloging differences.
